Saul rescues Jabesh-gilead (verses 1–11)

Saul's first great act as king was to rescue Jabesh-gilead from the Ammonites.

People may be willing to surrender their freedom, or even lose their eyes, to save their earthly lives.

Would it not be wiser to surrender a cherished sin, however dear to us—like our right eye—rather than be cast into the fire of judgment?

Notice Saul's faith and confidence.

From that faith came his courage and determination.

Notice also how actively he carried out the work.

When the Lord's Spirit comes upon people, he can make them skillful even when they lack experience.

When zeal for God's glory and love for brothers and sisters move us to energetic service, and the Lord is pleased to help, great results can follow very quickly.

Saul's kingship is confirmed (verses 12–15)

The people who had despised Saul now honored him.

Turning an enemy into a friend benefits us more than killing that enemy.

One day everyone will acknowledge the Savior they once despised as the Lord's Anointed King.

For now, Christ receives repentant rebels at his mercy seat.

He even intercedes for them.

But the day is approaching when he will sit upon the throne of righteous judgment and condemn those who persist in opposing him.

Samuel bears witness to his integrity (verses 1–5)

Samuel not only cleared his own character; he also gave Saul an example and reminded the people how ungrateful they had been both to God and to Samuel.

Everyone owes a proper duty to a good reputation, particularly those serving in public offices.

They should protect it from unjust accusations and suspicions, so that they may complete their work with honor as well as joy.

When we know we have acted honestly in our responsibilities, that knowledge can comfort us even if others treat us with contempt or ingratitude.

Samuel reminds Israel of God's justice (verses 6–15)

Ministers must reason with those they teach.

It is not enough simply to exhort people or give instructions.

They should seek to persuade, convince the mind and thus win both the will and the affections.

Samuel reminded Israel of the righteous works God had done for the people.

The Lord will enable those who continue to follow him faithfully to go on following him.

But disobedience would bring certain ruin upon Israel.

We are deeply mistaken if we suppose we can escape God's justice merely by refusing his authority.

Even if we declare that he will not rule us, he will still judge us.

God sends thunder during the wheat harvest (verses 16–25)

At Samuel's word the Lord sent thunder and rain during the wheat harvest, a season when such weather was highly unusual in that country.

The storm occurred on a clear day.

Samuel also announced it in advance.

The unusual timing and prophecy together convinced Israel of the wrong it had done in demanding a king.

The people had expected more from human strength than from God's power or Samuel's prayers.

Could their new king command a storm as the prophet could through prayer?

They were deeply shaken.

Some sinners will not recognize their guilt until God confronts them through the storm and thunder of severe providence.

Israel begged Samuel to pray for the people.

Now they recognized their need of the man they had recently disregarded.

Likewise, people who refuse Christ's rule over their lives may still wish to have him intercede for them to turn away God's wrath.

Samuel's goal was to strengthen Israel's faith.

Anything we make into a god will eventually disappoint us.

Created things are good in their proper place, but they become empty substitutes when we put them in God's place.

It is sinful to abandon prayer, and especially to stop praying for God's church.

The people asked Samuel to pray, but he promised something more: he would also teach them.

He gave two reasons for faithful service.

Gratitude, because God had already done such great things for them.

And their own welfare, because they must consider what would happen if they continued in wrongdoing.

As a faithful watchman, Samuel warned them and thereby fulfilled his own responsibility before God.

When we remember God's great acts—above all the work of redemption—we need never lack reasons, encouragement or help for serving him.

Saul reigned for a year without any remarkable events.

In his second year, the events in this chapter occurred.

For more than a year, he had allowed the Philistines time to prepare for war and weaken and disarm the Israelites.

When people grow proud and trust their own sufficiency, they often make foolish decisions.

The enemies of God's people gain many of their best opportunities through the misconduct of those who claim to be the people's friends.

When Saul finally sounded the alarm, the Israelites were dissatisfied with his leadership or terrified by the enemy's strength.

Many failed to come to his aid, and others soon deserted him.

Saul offers an unlawful sacrifice (verses 8–14)

Saul broke the specific instruction Samuel had given about what to do in an emergency (1 Samuel 10:8).

He offered the sacrifice himself without Samuel.

But Saul was neither a priest nor a prophet.

When challenged about his disobedience, he defended himself and showed no repentance.

He wanted to present a rebellious act as prudent leadership and genuine religious devotion.

People who lack inward godliness often place great importance on outward acts of worship.

Samuel told Saul that he had harmed himself.

Those who disobey God's commands act foolishly against their own good.

Sin is folly, and people deeply committed to it are deeply foolish.

Our response to seemingly small matters often reveals whether our hearts truly desire to obey God.

Human observers might consider Saul's act a minor offense.

But the Lord saw the unbelief and distrust, contempt for divine authority and justice, and rebellion against conscience that lay behind it.

Blessed Savior, may we never bring you our poor offerings or imagined peace offerings without trusting in your precious, entirely sufficient sacrifice.

You alone have made peace for us through the blood of your cross.

The Philistines keep Israel without weapons (verses 15–23)

The Philistines acted cleverly when they gained the advantage.

They not only prevented the Israelites from making weapons.

They forced them to depend upon their enemies even for the tools needed to cultivate the land.

Saul had acted foolishly by failing to correct this danger when his reign began.

Lack of true judgment accompanies lack of grace.

Sins that seem small to us may have very dangerous consequences.

How miserable a guilty, defenseless nation is!

Yet even more miserable are those who lack the whole armor of God.

Saul receives judgment against Amalek (verses 1–9)

God had announced judgment on the Amalekites long before (Exodus 17:14; Deuteronomy 25:19).

That judgment was delayed until their sins had reached their full measure.

Henry insists that the righteous Lord does no injustice.

The Kenites' ancestors had shown kindness to Israel.

God remembered that kindness and spared their descendants, even while judging Amalek for its ancestors' cruelty.

Henry sees this contrast as evidence of divine justice in this exceptional historical judgment.

It is dangerous to remain in the company of people under God's judgment.

We should separate from their wrongdoing rather than share in their sins and plagues (Revelation 18:4).

God's command to Saul was explicit and tested his obedience.

Saul's failure revealed a proud and rebellious heart.

He destroyed only the animals and goods that were least valuable.

He kept the better things for himself.

The things destroyed were understood in the narrative as given over to divine judgment.

The ancient command is described here as a historical act of judgment, not a license for private violence or a modern religious campaign.

Samuel confronts Saul's self-justification (verses 10–23)

When Scripture speaks of God repenting, Henry explains that this does not mean God changes his mind as people do.

It means a change in the way God deals with people.

The change was in Saul: he had turned away from following the Lord.

Through his rebellion, he made God his enemy.

Samuel prayed for Saul through an entire night.

The rejection of sinners grieves believers.

God does not delight in their death, and neither should we.

Saul boasted that he had obeyed.

Sinners often try to escape God's judgment by defending themselves.

But the sound of the animals Saul had spared spoke against him, like rust testifying against a hoarder (James 5:3).

People often claim to obey God while their indulgence of sinful desires, love of the world, angry and unkind attitudes, and neglect of holy responsibilities testify otherwise.

Consider how much harm arises from greed!

The deepest evil of sin is disobedience to God.

Saul's hearts—and ours when ruled by fleshly desires—try to excuse disobedience by presenting it as something pleasing or useful.

It is difficult to persuade the disobedient that they are wrong.

But God values humble, sincere, conscientious obedience more than any burnt offering or sacrifice.

Obedience honors God and requires us to deny ourselves more than a visible ceremony does.

It is much easier to bring an animal to the altar than to bring every proud thought and our whole will into submission to God.

People unwilling to submit to God's rule are unworthy to rule other human beings.

Saul's confession is insincere (verses 24–31)

Henry identifies three signs of hypocrisy in Saul's repentance.

First, Saul sought Samuel's approval and forgiveness, appearing more anxious about Samuel's opinion and favor than God's.

Second, he continued making excuses even while admitting wrongdoing.

That is not the response of genuine repentance.

Third, he cared chiefly about preserving his reputation and influence among the people.

Human beings are changeable and weak.

They alter their plans, fail to accomplish what they intend, and meet events they could not foresee.

But God is not like that.

The Strength of Israel does not lie or fail.

Samuel judges Agag and mourns Saul (verses 32–35)

Many people imagine that their greatest danger is past when it is actually near.

They put the thought of death and judgment far away.

Samuel called Agag to account for his own evil acts.

Agag had followed the cruelty of his ancestors, and Henry understands the judgment upon him as reckoning with that history of bloodshed.

Saul seemed unconcerned that God had rejected him.

But Samuel grieved for Saul continually.

In a similar way, Jerusalem remained comfortably careless while Christ wept over it.

Do we truly desire to do all God's will?

Let us turn to him, not merely with outward forms and appearances, but sincerely.

We often form a mistaken judgment of characters; but the Lord values only the faith, fear, and love, which are planted in the heart, beyond human discernment. And God does not favour our children according to our fond partiality, but often most honours and blesses those who have been least regarded. David at length was pitched upon. Do we behave wisely in every part of our lives?

Are there avoidable failures of duty, rash words or sinful reactions in us?

Other people's stubbornness or unfair treatment never justifies sinful anger in ourselves.
